positions.commentary: Charlie Munger said Costco is a business that does a very good job for its shareholders.

thesis: This episode argues that exceptional businesses are defined by their ability to benefit all stakeholders—customers, employees, vendors, and shareholders—rather than just financial metrics. It highlights Costco as a rare model that performs extremely well for investors, while contrasting it with Conwood, a financially attractive but ethically rejected business due to its harmful nature.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger viewed Costco as an exceptional business model that benefits all stakeholders including customers, shareholders, employees, and vendors.
claims.quote: Charlie referred to Costco as the ultimate win, win, win, win business model. So it is a business that does an exceptionally good job for all its customers. It is a business that does a very good job for its shareholders. It is a business that does a really good job for its employees. It's a business that does a very good job for its vendors.

claims.claim: Costco's business model is rare and tends to perform extremely well for investors.
claims.quote: These win-win business models are very rare. And these win-win business models tend to do extremely well for investors. So one of the things to look for when you're looking at different businesses is try to look at is it win-win, is it win-win, is it win-lose?

claims.claim: Costco's hourly rates are significantly higher than Walmart's, and they promote from within, with the current CEO starting as a forklift operator.
claims.quote: Costco's hourly rates are 50% more than Walmart, for example. Their employee turnover is much lower than all of the retailers. They heavily promote from within. In fact, the present CEO of Costco started as a forklift operator. And he moved all the way up to now CEO of this large company.
